2.text: The shamanistic “spirits” are very ill tempered, especially toward the

3.text: shaman with whom they are connected. If he does not carry out implicitly

4.text: all the suggestions they make about his dress, mode of living, and the details

5.text: of ceremonials, they become angry and chastise him, or punish him otherwise.

6.text: If he continues to disobey, they kill him. If the “spirits” are displeased with

7.text: any of the listeners at a ceremony, they usually take vengeance on the

8.text: shaman. For this reason, outsiders must be very quiet, and careful not to

9.text: pry into the work of the “spirits.”

10.text: On the other hand, when the shaman has kept faithfully his compact

11.text: with the “spirits,” they must come at his call, and must assist him in all

12.text: troubles and difficulties. “These are my people, my own little ‘spirits,’” said

13.text: one shaman when I expressed a doubt as to whether his “spirits” would come

14.text: or not. “They will not leave me, but will seek me all the time, as a fawn

16.text: Stories of Chukchee folk-lore are full of episodes in which shamanistic

17.text: “spirits” come at the call of the shaman when he is in difficulty, and deliver

18.text: him from imminent peril. One old shaman, Aˊñɪka by name, who lived in

19.text: the village of Nuˊnlig̣ren, told me that when he was still newly inspired, he

20.text: happened to travel by sea in a skin boat with seven other men, all of whom

21.text: were shamans, and each one older than himself. Suddenly the boat sprung a

22.text: leak. The owner, who was steering, exclaimed, “Stop that leak, some of you!”

23.text: but no one was able to do anything. Then he himself called a “seaweed-

24.text: spirit” who happened to be among his supernatural assistants, and told him

25.text: to stick to the leak. Thus the boat came to shore. When they were near

26.text: to the landing, Aˊñɪka exclaimed, “I have done enough in taking care of

27.text: you (by stopping the leak)! Now, if you are really shamans, save yourselves

28.text: from destruction!” The “seaweed-spirit” dropped off, and the boat began to

29.text: sink. Aˊñɪka and the owner of the boat were able to reach the shore by

30.text: swimming, but all the others were drowned.

31.text: This story is analogous in many respects to a folk-lore story that I

32.text: collected in the village of Čeˊčin. In that story also, a young shaman with

33.text: the aid of a “seaweed-spirit” saves a boat. Then he bids defiance to those

34.text: in the boat, and, suddenly turning into a hawk, seizes the boat-owner and

35.text: carries him to land, while all the others perish.

36.text: Shamanistic “spirits,” as a rule, do not like one another. When they

37.text: meet near a shaman, they are said to quarrel and to abuse one another in

38.text: a most violent manner. The shaman, however, brings about a reconciliation,

39.text: and prevails upon them to act harmoniously. Thus, in the story of the

40.text: “Two Rival Shamans,” the house of one of them is covered on all sides

41.text: with a number of “spirits,” and a “spirit” of another shaman, who comes for

42.text: assault, cannot find an opening through which to enter.¹
